Sparsely vegetated (<10% cover) rock, slopes, and badlands occurring in arid and semiarid canyons, basins, and foothills. Landforms include cliff and canyon walls, bedrock outcrops, steep mesa and plateau breaks, scree, and talus. Sites include shale outcrops, clayey badlands, and volcanic deposits such as lava, cinder, ash, tuff, and basalt. Some substrates are alkaline or saline, which chemically limits plant growth. Badlands often have clay soils that reduce water infiltration, increasing erosion and limiting moisture and nutrient availability.Most occurrences of this habitat are on sparsely vegetated rock or unique soil outcrops and remain unaltered. Where soil is present in this habitat, it has minimal cover of stabilizing perennial vegetation and biological soil crusts, making it particularly vulnerable to disturbance. Associated, dependent, near-obligate, or obligate SWAP species include Western Spotted Skunk, California Bighorn Sheep, 3 bat species (Western Small-footed Myotis, Pallid Bat, Spotted Bat), American Pika, Dwarf Shrew, Great Basin Collared Lizard, a metallic wood-boring beetle (Chrysobothris horningi), Marbled Disc, Packard's Milk-vetch, Winward's Goldenbrush, and Nez Perce Monkey-flower. Cliff, Scree & Badland Sparse Vegetation has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S5 and there are 35 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, 4 of which are obligates (Appendix 5).

perennial streams occur across the state. They range from subalpine headwaters fed by snowmelt to montane streams with both snow and spring sources, to foothill spring-fed streams. These subalpine and montane streams are cold (<54 °F [<12 °C]) and narrow (<7 ft [<2 m]), with flows ranging from spring pulses to minimal groundwatersupported flows in summer. Streams often originate at lakes or ponds in subalpine cirques. Other streams are sustained by springs.Many small perennial streams in montane and subalpine locations remain minimally altered by human activities. However, changes in precipitation and hydrologic regimes may decrease the condition of these habitats and negatively affect cold-waterdependent biotic communities. At lower elevations, various stressors may reduce aquatic habitat extent and condition. Associated, dependent, nearobligate, or obligate SWAP species include Rocky Mountain Tailed Frog, Coeur d'Alene Salamander, Harlequin Duck, Black Swift, Olive-sided Flycatcher, Silver-haired Bat, 4 sculpin species (Wood River, Slimy, Shoshone, Cedar), Green Sucker, Leopard Dace, Chinook Salmon (Snake River spring/summer-run ESU), Harvestman genus Acuclavella species group, numerous species of snowfly and caddisfly, Pilose Crayfish, and Idaho Amphipod. Small Streams (1st, 2nd order) -Perennial has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S3 and there are 58 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, 19 of which are obligates (Appendix 5).

These are nonflowing (or minimally flowing in run-of-river reservoirs) open water habitats with <30% vegetative cover. Lakes and ponds occupy topographic depressions. They encompass a range of sizes, depths, and origins. They include lakes and ponds in subalpine cirques, montane lakes contained by glacial moraines, kettle ponds, oxbow ponds, and spring-fed ponds. Reservoirs occur in river and stream channels, or on natural lakes impounded by dams, with their size and shape determined by topography. They also occupy depressions created by dikes or excavation (mining). They range from expansive reservoirs on rivers to small livestock ponds, wildlife habitat ponds, or urban stormwater basins.Most remote, subalpine lakes and ponds are minimally altered by human activities. Lower elevation lakes, ponds, and reservoirs vary in condition. Associated, dependent, near-obligate, or obligate SWAP species include Northern Leopard Frog, Northern Pintail, Black Tern, Caspian Tern, American Bittern, Common Loon, American White Pelican, Clark's and Western grebes, Fringed Myotis, 3 whitefish species (Pygmy, Bonneville, Bear Lake), Lake Chub, Bull Trout, Bear Lake Sculpin, Raptor Fairy Shrimp, and Columbia Primitive Minnow Mayfly. Lakes, Ponds & Reservoirs has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S4 and there are 54 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, 20 of which are obligates (Appendix 5).

ecosystems formed where water flows from the ground. They support unique communities of aquatic biota, including plants. Productive riparian and wetland habitats are associated with springs. The aquifers supplying springs are recharged by surface water and precipitation. Springs occur where water discharges from slopes at faults and rock fractures or when forced to the surface by impermeable layers, or thermal or pressure gradients (artesian springs).

Habitats (not mapped due to the sensitivity of locations) include both natural caves as well as abandoned mines. Because many of the abandoned mines have not been active for the past 50 to 100 years, and provide many of the same features as natural caves, a diverse array of wildlife species (especially bats) have colonized them. Most caves occur in the southern part of the state. Idaho does not have much karst (limestone region marked by sinks, abrupt ridges, irregular protuberant rocks, caverns, and underground streams) habitat. Most caves are lava tube caves, formed by volcanic eruptions where the low pressure lava developed a thick, hard crust. These types of caves occur in south-central Idaho across the Snake River Plain. Some Idaho caves are ice caves.

Recreational opportunities within this province include angling, hunting, boating, hiking, camping, horseback riding, wildlife watching, and winter activities such as skiing and snowmobiling. Two of the 5 federally recognized American Indian tribes in Idaho are based in this area: the Coeur d'Alene Tribe (Schitsu'umsh) in Plummer and the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho in Bonners Ferry.

figure.figDesc: Boise and lower Payette River valleys, generally called the Treasure Valley. This area is characterized by urban and suburban development as well as extensive areas devoted to agricultural production of crops for both human and livestock use. Other major population centers within the province include Twin Falls, Pocatello, and Idaho Falls.The aridity of this region requires water management programs, including water storage, delivery, and regulation for agricultural, commercial, and residential uses. Agricultural fields are irrigated with water mostly supplied by diversion from the Snake, Boise, and Payette rivers.

note.p: Major hydroelectric reservoirs on the Snake River include CJ Strike, Swan Falls, Lake Walcott, and American Falls Reservoir. Reaches of the Boise and Payette rivers within the province are controlled by upstream dams. BLM, and state-owned lands administered by IDL. Other major land managers in the province include the 890 mi² (2,305 km²) Idaho National Laboratory (INL), operated by the US Department of Energy (DOE), and the more than 1,172 mi² (3,035 km²) Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve (CRMO), cooperatively managed by the National Park Service (NPS) and BLM. Finally, 2 federally-recognized American Indian tribes own lands within the province: the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation, Idaho, and the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of the Duck Valley Reservation, Nevada.

figure.figDesc: Within this plan, species are presented in a phylogenetic sequence from phylum to family as currently understood. Arrangement of the classes, orders, and families generally follows the American Fisheries Society's 8th edition of Common and Scientific Names of Fishes from the United States, Canada, and Mexico(Page et al. 2023) for fishes, the Society for the Study of Amphibians and Reptiles(Bonett et al. 2017) for amphibians and reptiles, the Mammal Diversity Database of the American Society of Mammalogists (ASM) (Mammal Diversity Database 2023) for mammals (except bats), Bat Species of the World (Simmons and Cirranello 2022B) for bats, American Ornithological Society's (AOS) Checklist of North and Middle

note.p: American Birds(Chesser et al. 2023) for birds,Hitchcock and Cronquist (2018) for vascularplants, and OpenTree et al. (2021) for nonvascular lichens, hornworts, liverworts, and mosses. Invertebrate phylogeny followsGiribet and Edgecombe (2020) for phylum, class, and order, and the Open Tree of Life current synthetic tree (OpenTree et al. 2021) for family. Within families, genera and species are listed alphabetically. Scientific and common names for fishes, amphibians and reptiles, mammals, bats, and birds follow these same taxonomic sources with some exceptions. For example, cutthroat trout (e.g., Yellowstone and Bonneville) classification followsMarkle (2018). In addition, we recognize the Northern Idaho Ground Squirrel (Urocitellus brunneus) and Southern Idaho Ground Squirrel (U. endemicus) as distinct species based on work byHoisington-Lopez et al. (2012). Because of the complexity of invertebrate taxonomy, we used multiple sources for both scientific and common names, including peerreviewed literature. Exceptions to this include freshwater mussels (Mollusca: Bivalvia: Unionida), which follow FMCS (2023a), and freshwater gastropods, which follow FMCS

Understories are often lush, structurally complex, and diverse, but vary depending on moisture
and disturbance. Tall deciduous shrubs, namely Western Serviceberry, Chokecherry, and
Scouler's Willow can be common, along with shorter Mountain Snowberry, Woods' Rose,
Mountain-box, Common Juniper, Mountain Big Sagebrush, or Creeping Oregon-grape. Typical
graminoids are Alaska Wheatgrass, Mountain Brome, Blue Wild-rye, needlegrasses, Wheeler's

especially tall species such as Fendler's Meadowrue, Sticky Purple Geranium, sweet-roots,
Silvery Lupine, Nettle-leaf Horse-mint, Western Valerian, Many-flowered Stickseed, Butterweed
Groundsel, Western Coneflower, Engelmann's Aster, and California False Hellebore. Shorter
forbs include Little False Solomon's Seal, Common Yarrow, Woodland Strawberry, Northern

note.p: Intact stands of this habitat are typically located in high-elevation watersheds, where they experience natural disturbance cycles (e.g., fire, avalanches). Lower elevation stands tend to be less productive, with less diverse understories, and at greater risk of dieback due to various stressors. Associated or dependent SWAP species include Sharp-tailed Grouse, Cassin's Finch, Cassia Crossbill, White-headed Woodpecker, Great Gray Owl, Moose, Grizzly Bear (Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem population), and Silver-haired Bat. Aspen Forest & Woodland has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S3 and there are 15 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, 1 of which is an obligate (Appendix 5).

Spruce. Whitebark Pine is a seral species, establishing after a disturbance such as wildfire or
avalanche. Although fire can be necessary to maintain Whitebark Pine habitat and Clark's
Nutcracker seed caching sites, varying intensity levels result in different impacts to Whitebark
Pine communities. For example, even low-intensity fire can kill individual trees if subjected to
bole scorching (FWS 2018). Fire intervals vary from 30 to 300 years (Tomback et al. 2001).
Most of this habitat has not been significantly altered by human land uses, although it is
particularly susceptible to disease, changing climate conditions, and other stressors.
Associated, dependent, near-obligate, or obligate SWAP species include Clark's Nutcracker,
Rocky Mountain Goat, Moose, Wolverine, Long-eared Myotis, American Pika, Hoary Marmot,
High Country Bumble Bee, Bloom Peak Douglasia, and Whitebark Pine. Whitebark Pine Forest
& Woodland has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S3 and there are 14 SWAP species for
which this habitat is important, 2 of which are obligates (Appendix 5).
The shrub understory is typically patchy, characterized by Common Juniper, Alpine Prickly
Currant, Canada Buffalo-berry, Mountain Snowberry, or Grouseberry. The herbaceous layer
ranges from sparse to a moderately dense cover of graminoids, including Spike-fescue, Idaho
Fescue, Geyer's and Ross's sedges, or Wheeler's Bluegrass. Forbs indicative of droughty,
poorly-developed soil are scattered, such as arnicas, lupines, Northern Goldenrod, Beargrass,
Common Yarrow, Little-leaf Pussy-toes, and Blueleaf Cinquefoil. Although birds and mammals
(e.g., Grizzly Bear and rodents) eat and cache Whitebark Pine seeds, Clark's Nutcracker is
almost exclusively the seed dispersal mechanism for the species (FWS 2018), transporting the
large, wingless seeds long distances and caching them across open subalpine habitat. In
suitable sites, Whitebark Pine regenerates in clusters from forgotten caches.

figure.head: 2014 Jessica Irwin Pinyon-Juniper Woodland
figure.figDesc: Minimally-disturbed stands of this habitat, characterized by widely-spaced, old, large-diameter trees with native plant understory communities, occur across south Idaho where fire has not been suppressed. Over the past 125 years or more, some areas have experienced increased juniper density in existing stands as well as expansion into shrub-steppe habitats. Associated or obligate SWAP species include Golden Eagle, Ferruginous Hawk, Pinyon Jay, Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch, Western Spotted Skunk, Canyon Bat, Pallid Bat, Pygmy Rabbit, Pygmy Shorthorned Lizard, and Elusive Polemonium. Pinyon-Juniper Woodland has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S4 and there are 25 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, 1 of which is an obligate (Appendix 5).

Open stands, maintained by fire, have a productive understory similar to mesic sagebrush
steppe in composition. Denser stands have sparser understories. Understory shrubs include
Big Sagebrush, Antelope-brush, rabbit-brushes, Low Sagebrush, Black Sagebrush, horse-
brushes, or Slenderbush Buckwheat, with Creambush Ocean-spray, goldenbrushes, or Spiny
Green-bush on rocks. Mesic sites may have Creeping Oregon-grape and deciduous shrubs
such as Mountain Snowberry, Wax Currant, serviceberries, or cherries. Herbaceous species
reflect soil (depth, texture, moisture) and environmental conditions (slope, aspect, lithology,
shade, disturbance). Common grasses include Bluebunch Wheatgrass, Idaho Fescue, Great
Basin Wildrye, Sandberg's Bluegrass, Indian Ricegrass, Needle-and-Thread, Salmon Wildrye,
needlegrasses, or Spike-fescue. Forbs can be diverse but typically have low cover and are
commonly represented by Arrowleaf Balsamroot, Wyeth Buckwheat, Mat Buckwheat, Silvery
Lupine, Rocky Mountain Helianthella, Long-leaf and Hood's phloxes, biscuit-roots, Longleaved
Hawksbeard, pricklypear cactus, Western Groundsel, cryptanthas, or Tapertip Onion.

SWAP species for which this habitat is important, none of which are obligates (Appendix 5).
Understory composition varies, depending on environmental setting. At higher elevations,
heath family shrubs, such as Trapper's Tea, Bog Blueberry, Grouseberry, and Red Mountain-
heath, are common. An array of tall deciduous shrubs is often present, especially on sunnier
streambanks, including Sitka and Mountain alders, Red-osier Dogwood, Drummond's and
Dusky willows, Fool's and Globe huckleberries, Rocky Mountain Maple, Western Serviceberry,
Douglas's Hawthorn, Swamp Gooseberry, Stinking Currant, Alder Buckthorn, Thimbleberry,
Common Snowberry, and Douglas's Spirea. Herbaceous layers can be diverse. Characteristic
graminoids include Bluejoint Reedgrass, Mountain, Southern Beaked, Water, and Soft-leaved
sedges, Blue Wild-rye, and Common Brome. Along with Lady-fern, robust forbs are
characteristic, such as Arrowleaf Groundsel, Clasping-leaved Twisted-stalk, Canby's Lovage,
Little False Solomon's Seal, Leafy-bracted Aster, Cow-parsnip, false hellebores, Sitka Burnet,
and Western Meadowrue. Low-growing forbs are common, including White Marsh-marigold
and Jeffrey's Shooting Star at high elevations, and Common Horsetail, False Bugbane, Alpine
Mitrewort, Sweetscented Bedstraw, Dwarf Enchanter's Nightshade, Blueleaf Strawberry, and

figure.head: Idaho Department of Fish & Game 50 Ruderal Flooded & Swamp Forest & Woodland
figure.figDesc: Swamp Forest & Woodland has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of SNA (i.e., conservation status rank is not applicable because the ecosystem is nonnative) and there are 8 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, none of which are obligates (Appendix 5). This habitat type is dominated by introduced invasive tree species. Abundant trees include Russian Olive, tamarisks, Silver Maple, Box-elder, Green Ash, Eastern and Fremont cottonwoods, White Poplar, White and Crack willows, Siberian and American elms, Black Locust, catalpas, White Mulberry, and fruit trees (e.g., cherries, apples, pears, Apricot). Invasive shrubs can be common, especially False Indigo, roses, and Himalayan Blackberry. Invasive plant species are also abundant in the understory such as the vine-like White Bryony and Bittersweet, grasses (e.g., Reed Canarygrass, Quackgrass, Smooth Brome, Meadow Foxtail, Creeping Bentgrass, Canada Bluegrass, Cheatgrass, Mouse Barley), and noxious weeds (e.g., Canada Thistle, Poison-hemlock, Pepperwort, Purple Loosestrife, Yellow Flag, Leafy Spurge, hound's-tongues). Other introduced ruderal species are common including Common Orache, Madwort, Curly Dock, lamb's quarters, Prickly Lettuce, Common Yellow Sweet-clover, and seeded Tall Wheatgrass. Relict or recovering native woody species, including Peach-leaf, Yellow, and Coyote willows, Golden Currant, Mountain Alder, Red-osier Dogwood, and Woods' Rose, are frequently intermixed but not dominant. Common native herbs, such as Woolly Sedge, Common Horsetail, Clasping-leaved Dogbane, goldenrods, and ruderal marsh species (e.g., Common Cat-tail, Hardstem Bulrush, Soft Rush, Common Duckweed), also occur.

row.cell: Low-elevation riparian forests and woodlands developing in human-altered or created settings. Stands occur along managed rivers, in disturbed floodplains, on reservoir fringes, around altered seeps and springs, on levees, along irrigation ditches and diversions, around created ponds and marshes, and in agricultural areas fed by irrigation. Associated SWAP species include Cinnamon Teal, Yellow-billed Cuckoo, Moose, Little Brown Myotis, Silver-haired Bat, Common Gartersnake, Western Bumble Bee, and Suckley Cuckoo Bumble Bee. figure.head: Idaho Department of Fish & Game 52 Temperate
figure.figDesc: & Boreal Grassland & ShrublandThese are mesic to seasonally dry upland habitats dominated by shrubs or herbaceous grasses or forbs. Tree cover is typically <10% and limited by a combination of drought, fire, or cold air pooling in valley bottom meadows. Soils are often well developed and productive. Habitats occur from canyons and foothills to subalpine zones. Where deciduous or evergreen shrubs (varying in height) dominate (with at least 10% to 20% cover), there is typically a diverse understory or intershrub herbaceous layer of grasses and forbs. Grasses may include both bunchgrass and sod-forming species, with annuals in disturbed areas. Forbs can be diverse and sometimes codominant with grasses. Except where disturbed, the ground surface varies from litter and duff to biological soil crusts.

Dominant and diagnostic species include naturalized forage grasses such as Smooth Brome,
Kentucky Bluegrass, bentgrasses, fescues, ryegrasses, Orchard-grass, Intermediate

dominated by roses, Scot's Broom, or Himalayan Blackberry. Native shrubs, grasses, and forbs
typical of Montane-Foothill Grassland & Shrubland habitat may be present with variable cover.
Although disturbed and composed of introduced species, this habitat still provides pollinator
and wildlife forage and security habitat.

row.cell: Low elevation, seasonally wet riparian shrublands,
meadows, marshes, and mudflats in valleys, plains, and
basins. This habitat occurs on flats, floodplains
margins, sloped seeps and springs, drainages, and
swales. Mudflats occur in drawdown zones of
waterbodies. Hydrology is supported by groundwater
or flooding. Meadows and pools are seasonally
flooded or saturated, while marshes can be
persistently flooded. Soils are fine-textured alluvium
with drainage impeded by underlying clay.
Many of Idaho's most productive and diverse low-
elevation marshes and meadows occur on WMAs such
as the Coeur d'Alene River and Camas Prairie-
Centennial Marsh. Examples of culturally important
camas meadows occur at Weippe Prairie and Duck
Valley. Other low-elevation seasonal wetlands are
often altered by human land uses, lack of disturbance,
and climate change. Associated, dependent, or
obligate SWAP species include Western Toad, Northern Leopard Frog, Columbia Spotted Frog
(Great Basin population), Northern Pintail, Trumpeter Swan, the migratory shorebird
assemblage, Black Tern, Greater Sage-Grouse, Sandhill Crane, Short-eared Owl, Moose,
Spotted Bat, Common Gartersnake, Yellow and Western bumble bees, Monarch Butterfly,
Indian Valley Sedge, Water Howellia, and Ute Ladies-tresses. Lowland Marsh, Wet Meadow &
Shrubland has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S3 and there are 28 SWAP species for
which this habitat is important, 1 of which is an obligate (Appendix 5).
Dominant shrubs include Mountain Alder, Douglas's Spirea, Douglas's Hawthorn, Red-osier
Dogwood, roses, willows, Common Snowberry, and Pacific Ninebark. The herb layer includes
Bluejoint Reedgrass, sedges, Fowl Mannagrass, Small-fruit Bulrush, Cow-parsnip, Stinging
Nettle, Arrowleaf Groundsel, Columbian Monkshood, Lady-fern, and Skunk Cabbage.
Graminoids dominate marshes, primarily bur-reeds, sedges, rushes, spike-rushes, bulrushes
(Hardstem Bulrush, Wool-grass), wild rices, mannagrasses, and Common Cat-tail. Forbs are
common, such as Water Horsetail, Purple Cinquefoil, Buckbean, beggar-ticks, bugleweeds,
arrowheads, Northern Water-plantain, Common Mare's-tail, loosestrifes, skullcaps, and
speedwells. Exposed mudflats support diverse mats of native and introduced annuals. Species
composition in meadows varies. California Oatgrass, Tufted Hairgrass, spike-rushes, Baltic and
Nevada rushes, Nebraska and Freeway sedges, Meadow Barley, Big Bluegrass, wildryes,
wheatgrasses, Mat Muhly, and Common Three-square are diagnostic graminoids. Forbs can
codominate, namely Common Camas, Northern Mule's-ears, ragworts, Slender Cinquefoil,
Western Blue Flag, Western Mugwort, clovers, docks, asters, yampahs, beardtongues, and
paintbrushes. Annuals are abundant and Silver Sagebrush is a locally abundant shrub.

figure.head: Idaho Department of Fish & Game 70 Montane Marsh, Wet Meadow & Shrubland
figure.figDesc: Diverse and productive native wet meadows, riparian shrublands, and marshes commonly occur throughout montane watersheds and subalpine areas across Idaho. In some areas, floodplain processes necessary for sustaining meadows and shrublands have been disrupted due to various stressors. Associated, dependent, or near-obligate SWAP species include Western Toad, Northern Leopard Frog, Trumpeter Swan, Sandhill Crane, Wilson's Warbler, Moose, Western Small-footed Myotis, Northern Bog Lemming, Common Gartersnake, Western Bumble Bee, Monarch Butterfly, Bodin's Milk-vetch, and Clearwater Phlox. Montane Marsh, Wet Meadow & Shrubland has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S3 and there are 27 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, none of which are obligates (Appendix 5).

Shrubs vary in height, reflecting hydrology and elevation. Willows (Booth's, Drummond's,
Geyer's, Bebb's, Lemmon's, Dusky), alders (Mountain, Sitka), Red-osier Dogwood, currants,
Alder Buckthorn, Douglas's Hawthorn, Douglas's Spirea, Rocky Mountain Maple, Trapper's Tea,
and Bearberry Honeysuckle are characteristic. Meadows support short-statured Bog Birch,
willows (Wolf's, Diamondleaf, Eastwood's), Shrubby Cinquefoil, Sweet-berry Honeysuckle, Red
Mountain-heath, and blueberries. Herbs vary depending on hydrology and soils. Dominant
graminoids are sedges (Water, Southern Beaked, Mountain, Short-beaked, Woodrush,
Nebraska, Woolly), Tufted Hairgrass, Bluejoint Reedgrass, Baltic Rush, Few-flowered Spike-
rush, Pullup Muhly, Small-fruit Bulrush, and mannagrasses. High elevations have sedges (Black
Alpine, Sheep) and rushes. Forbs can be conspicuous and include Jeffrey's Shooting Star,
Globe Penstemon, Pink Elephants, lovages, bistorts, marsh-marigolds, camases, Plantainleaved
Buttercup, Cleft-leaf and Arrowleaf groundsels, cinquefoils, Great Northern and Leafy-bracted
asters, Flat-top Pussy-toes, false hellebores, Lyall's Angelica, Cow-parsnip, Wandering Daisy,
paintbrushes, Stinging Nettle, monkshoods, Little False Solomon's Seal, Lady-fern, horsetails,
Bog St. John's-wort, claytonias, Large-leaved Avens, bedstraws, and Dwarf Enchanter's
Nightshade. Marshes, flooded more deeply and persistently, form around beaver ponds, lakes,
and depressions. Spike-Rushes, Kellogg's and Inflated sedges, and bur-reeds are common.

figure.head: Lowland-Foothill Riparian Shrubland Shrublands
figure.figDesc: associated with foothill, canyon, basin, and lower montane permanent, intermittent, or ephemeral streams and rivers. These habitats occur in semiarid and warm regions. Stands occur in steep, v-shaped valleys and canyons, or in broad and flat alluvial river valleys. They can be extensive on river floodplains or form narrow bands along small tributaries. Substrates are often sandy, gravelly, and cobbly alluvium found on islands, bars, banks, and terraces. Shrublands also occur around springs and seeps, along backwater and side channels, and on margins of swales, interdune depressions, beaver ponds, marshes, and wetlands. Many shrubs require flooding and bare alluvium for establishment. Most stands are maintained by annual flooding (seasonal or irregular). The water table is usually just below the surface for at least part of the growing season.Many examples of functioning riparian shrublands with native vegetation occur in less-developed foothill valleys across Idaho. However, the condition of this habitat in many locations has been impacted by various human land uses, changes in hydrology, invasive plant species, and climate change. Associated or dependent SWAP species include Woodhouse's Toad, Great Basin Spadefoot, Common Nighthawk, Mountain Quail, Greater Sage-Grouse, Western Spotted Skunk, Moose, Long-legged Myotis, Common Gartersnake, Western Bumble Bee, Monarch Butterfly, Gillette's Checkerspot, Least Bladdery Milk-vetch, Indian Valley Sedge, and Ute Ladies-tresses. Lowland-Foothill Riparian Shrubland has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-

are willows (Coyote, Arroyo, Yellow, Whiplash, Dusky), Water Birch, Mountain Alder, Douglas's
and River hawthorns, Woods' Rose, Lewis's Mock Orange, Chokecherry, Common Snowberry,
Golden Currant, Red-osier Dogwood, Rocky Mountain Maple, Lemonade Sumac, Western
Poison Ivy, Hairy Goldaster, sagebrushes, and introduced False Indigo. Herbs vary depending
on shrub density and flood disturbance. The most abundant species are Blue Wild-rye, Fowl

Red Columbine, asters, Cow-parsnip, Western Mugwort, Common Willow-herb, Large-leaved
Avens, and bedstraws. Less common grasses include Great Basin Wildrye, Fowl Bluegrass, and
wheatgrasses. Presence of Black Cottonwood indicates succession toward riparian forest.

Alkali-Saline Marsh, Playa & Shrubland has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S3 and there
are 9 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, none of which are obligates (Appendix
Dense to open shrublands occupying sites with deeper groundwater are dominated by Black
Greasewood, mixed with rabbit-brushes, Green Molly, saltbushes, Shrubby Cinquefoil (east
Idaho), willows, and rarely Iodine Bush. Trees, such as Russian Olive or Limberpine, are
marginal. The herbaceous understory and adjacent mesic meadows are characterized by
Saltgrass, Alkali Sacaton, sedges (Freeway, Parry's), Baltic Rush, Western Wheatgrass,
Beardless Wildrye, Great Basin Wildrye, Big Bluegrass, Slimstem Reedgrass, barleys, or seeded
Tall Wheatgrass. Forbs are not abundant in greasewood and include Showy Milkweed,
Common Yarrow, Alkali-mallow, and Poverty-weed. Seasonally flooded or saturated marshes
and wet meadows are dominated by a mix of bulrushes (American Three-square, Common
Three-square, Seacoast Tuberous Bulrush, Nevada Clubrush), Walking Spike-rush, Saltgrass,
alkaligrasses, Alkali Muhly, Alkali Cordgrass, Short-beaked Sedge, Seaside Arrow-grass,
Torrey's Rush, and Rabbitsfoot Grass. Characteristic forbs include Pahute Weed, Saltwort,
Silverweed, Short-rayed Aster, Swamp Milkweed, Cut-leaved Water Parsnip, Western
Centaury, and occasionally Red Glasswort and Alkali Plantain. Eastern Idaho calcareous seep-
fed meadows host a suite of uncommon forbs, including the globally rare Alkaline Primrose

note.p: Although Black Greasewood is widely distributed, alkaline-saline wet meadows and marshes dominated by native vegetation are less common but can be found on some WMAs (e.g., Market Lake, CJ Strike), wildlife habitat areas (WHAs) (e.g., Roswell Marsh), or NWRs (e.g., Bear Lake). Associated or dependent SWAP species include Northern Pintail, Cinnamon Teal, Greater Sage-Grouse, Sandhill Crane, Dark Kangaroo Mouse, Kelsey's Phlox (subsp. glandulosa), Nevada Goldenrod, and xanthoparmelia lichen (Xanthoparmelia norchlorochroa).

Areas of open bare soil or biological soil crusts may occur between plants.

figure.head: Dwarf Sagebrush Steppe & Shrubland
figure.figDesc: Extensive areas of intact habitat dominated by native species occur on plateaus, ridges, and slopes across southern Idaho. Many of these areas have rocky-clayey soils with naturally lower productivity that are resistant to annual grass invasion; however, they can be vulnerable to soil compaction. Associated, dependent, near-obligate, or obligate SWAP species include Great Basin Spadefoot, Common Nighthawk, Golden Eagle, Ferruginous Hawk, Greater Sage-Grouse, Burrowing Owl, Pronghorn, Big Brown Bat, Pygmy Rabbit, Dark Kangaroo Mouse, Southern Idaho Ground Squirrel, Great Basin Collared Lizard, Pygmy Short-horned Lizard, Idaho Point-headed Grasshopper, Yellow Bumble Bee, Columbia Oregonian, and Winward's Goldenbrush. Dwarf Sagebrush Steppe & Shrubland has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S4 and there are 34 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, 2 of which are obligates (Appendix 5).

row.cell: Xeric dwarf shrubland steppe found on
benches, gravelly alluvial fans and flats, and
gravelly or rocky slopes. Stands occur
across drier regions of Idaho, from low

(frequently basalt or rhyolite) and can be
Dwarf sagebrush species and herb cover varies according to soil and climate. Black Sagebrush
is widespread, occurring on gravelly, calcareous soils. Low Sagebrush also occurs widely, but
on shallow, fine-textured soils over bedrock or pan that impedes drainage. Fringed Sagebrush
can occur at higher elevations. Adapted to poor drainage and spring saturation, Low
Sagebrush (subsp. longiloba) occurs on shallow, alkaline, clayey soils, while Stiff Sagebrush is
found on shallow lithic soils over basalt in western Idaho including areas of mounded
topography. On scabland sites, shrubby buckwheats (Thyme Buckwheat, Round-headed
Eriogonum) are locally dominant. Other shrubs can be present or codominant, including
Antelope-brush, Big Sagebrush, Spiny Hopsage, and saltbushes, especially on deep soil
mounds. Herbaceous cover is lowest on scabland sites. Characteristic bunchgrasses include
Sandberg's Bluegrass, Idaho Fescue, Bluebunch Wheatgrass, Indian Ricegrass, Bottlebrush,
One-spike Wild Oatgrass, Thurber's Needlegrass, and introduced Bulbous Bluegrass. Forbs
include cushion, woody-based, and deeply taprooted species such as Hooker's Balsamroot,
Barestemmed, Gumbo, Gray's, and Wyeth biscuit-roots, Hood's Phlox, fleabanes, goldenweeds,
Big-head Clover, pussy-toes, Crag Ankle-aster, Gairdner's Penstemon, onions, rockcresses,
Gairdner's Yampah, paintbrushes, hawksbeards, and stonecrops. Annuals, such as knotweeds,
may be seasonally common. Moss and lichen cover is high in undisturbed areas.

figure.figDesc: Sandwort, cinquefoils, Parry's Clover), and the dwarf shrub Fringed Sagebrush. Fell-fields are dominated by hairy or thickly cutinized cushion or matted plants. Characteristic forbs include Pacific Sagewort, Cushion Phlox, Gordon's Ivesia, locoweeds (Oxytropis spp.), Oval-leaved Eriogonum, Moss Campion, spring parsleys, Old-man-of-the-mountain, forget-me-nots, fleabanes, Skunk Polemonium, whitlow-grasses, saxifrages, American Thorough-Wax, Alpine Hulsea, and spike-mosses. Caespitose grasses, such as Drummond's Rush, fescues (Alpine, Idaho), bluegrasses (Alpine, Glaucous), Purple Reedgrass, and Spike-fescue, occur. Heath family shrubs (e.g., Mertens's Mountain-heather, mountain-heaths, Western Bog Laurel, blueberries) or willows (Arctic, Snow; <0.5 m tall) characterize dwarf-shrublands. The herb layer includes turf and mesic species such as sedges (Dark Alpine, Payson's), Tufted Hairgrass, White Marsh-marigold, Alpine Bistort, Partridgefoot, Woolly Pussy-toes, Alpine Aster, and Creeping Sibbaldia. Patchy dwarf shrubs, namely Hooker's Mountain-avens and Shrubby Goldenbrush, occur on scree slopes with scattered bunchgrasses and forbs.

figure.figDesc: native, wetland, or xeriscape gardens that may provide habitat for pollinators. A wide variety of structure and growth forms may occur and provide habitat for a variety of SWAP species. Plants vary in spatial distribution, often fragmented by trails and infrastructure. This habitat is distinguished by frequent, repeated intensive management and maintenance, including mowing, clipping, pest and weed control, fertilization, and irrigation. Associated, dependent, near-obligate, or obligate SWAP species include Woodhouse's Toad, Trumpeter Swan, Black Tern, Franklin's Gull, White-faced Ibis, Ferruginous Hawk, Sandhill Crane, Bobolink, Loggerhead Shrike, Wilson's Warbler, Western Spotted Skunk, Moose, Silverhaired Bat, Common Gartersnake, Morrison and Western bumble bees, and Monarch Butterfly. Agricultural Vegetation has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of SNA and there are 34 total SWAP species for which this habitat is important, 1 of which is an obligate. Lawn, Garden & Recreational Vegetation has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of SNA and there are 15 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, none of which are obligates (Appendix 5).

note.p: Lawn, Garden & Recreational Vegetation occurs in developed areas. Vegetation includes designed, managed, and maintained grassy lawns, open woodlands, and shrub patches planted for recreation and aesthetics, and erosion control. This habitat occurs in parks, landscaped gardens, open space, and golf courses; around schools, institutions, homes, and commercial development; and along greenbelts, recreational trails, and stormwater detention ponds. Vegetation is characterized by nonnative, often ornamental plants, but may also

Freshwater Aquatic Vegetation has a habitat relative status (i.e., S-rank) of S3 and there are 12 SWAP species for which this habitat is important, 7 of which are obligates (Appendix 5).Floating leaf and rooted species may dominate at high elevations and in northern Idaho, such as Spatterdock, Water-shield, Broad-leaf Pondweed, and bur-reeds (Narrowleaf, Small). Freefloating species, such as mosquito-ferns, duckweeds, and Greater Duckweed, are abundant in nutrient rich water. figure.figDesc: Collaborate with local governments, resource managers, and other stakeholders to develop and implement actions that incentivize development in areas with low SGCN value and high development value for landowners and local communities. • Protect sensitive or vulnerable animal and plant SGCN populations and their habitats. • Support community, business, and industry efforts to implement mitigation for habitats affected by development. • Incentivize landowners to conserve and manage strategic parcels to benefit priority SGCN populations or habitats and sustain Idaho's natural resource-based economy, culture and heritage, and community amenities (e.g., Forest Legacy Program and Forest Stewardship Program). • Include land trusts as key partners in development of conservation easements in SGCN habitats that prevent development incompatible with SGCN and habitats.

figure.head: Game 125 Voluntary Actions Related to Outreach •
figure.figDesc: Promote and incentivize SGCN conservation education and fish-and-wildlife-related recreation.• Participate with communities, local governments, and development stakeholders in local comprehensive planning processes to share SGCN conservation goals and opportunities. • Partner with communities and local governments to create guidelines and BMPs designed to reduce human-wildlife conflict resulting from activities such as wildlife feeding, free-ranging pets, landscaping, and unsecured garbage (e.g.,IUCN 2023). • Conduct community outreach events to provide information about coexisting with wildlife in urban, suburban, and rural-residential settings. • Promote pollinator-friendly landscaping where appropriate to benefit pollinators including Monarch Butterfly and bumble bees (e.g., flowering plants, appropriate nesting habitat, nest-building materials, and appropriate landforms). • Develop and distribute information for landowners about landscaping plants that are poisonous to wildlife (e.g., ornamental yews such as Japanese, Common, Chinese, and Canada yews). • Encourage landscaping with plants that are not edible where wildlife is unwelcome. • Participate in collaborative programs that involve stakeholders in resource stewardship including SGCN conservation.

Development that expands WUIs can also worsen the condition of SGCN habitat caused by other Forest & Woodland habitat stressors. Actions that conserve SGCN by comprehensively addressing Forest & Woodland habitat stressors can also benefit communities (e.g., by protecting open space for outdoor recreation and reducing wildfire risks in the WUI). Depending on circumstances, the Idaho Department of Water Resources (IDWR) and US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) might regulate development in riparian forests per the Idaho Stream Channel Protection Act (ISCPA) and US Clean Water Act (CWA), respectively (see IDWR 2022b). Therefore, development in riparian forests might need state and federal permits that could include protective measures for SGCN. Examples of SGCN occurring in Forest & Woodland habitats and potentially influenced by development include Wolverine, Rocky Mountain Goat, Moose, Yellow-billed Cuckoo, Great Gray Owl, Lewis's Woodpecker, Clark's Nutcracker, Cassin's Finch, Western Bumble Bee, and Ute Ladies-tresses. Proposed voluntary actions intended to address the negative effects of stressors if occurring, and thus benefit SGCN conservation, responsible development, and valued community amenities, are listed in Table 3.1.1.

figure.figDesc: Development in Idaho's growing urban, suburban, and rural communities is often associated with Aquatic Vegetation & Freshwater Habitat (hereafter aquatic habitat), which can be important sources of water for domestic, municipal, and commercial uses, irrigation, and outdoor recreation. Development has the potential to reduce the quantity and quality of aquatic habitat near communities. In addition to development, other stressors potentially affecting aquatic habitat include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, shifting seasonal water runoff patterns, pollutants decreasing water quality through stormwater runoff and facility discharges, surface water and groundwater diversions, and the introduction and spread of invasive species. These interacting stressors can further affect both SGCN habitat and important amenities that aquatic habitat provides to communities. Shoreline and in-water development can also reduce SGCN habitat and worsen other potential stressors negatively affecting aquatic habitat for communities.

Idaho's water allocation and distribution processes administered by IDWR regulate the diversion of public waters for domestic, municipal, and commercial use. IDPES and NPDES permits include pollutant measures to meet water quality standards. The Western Governors' Association(WGA) Policy Resolution 2021-03, National Forest and Rangeland Management(WGA 2021a), emphasizes the importance of collaboration and strategic planning among stakeholders. Many longstanding partners associated with agriculture are already contributing greatly to conserving the state's fish, wildlife, and plants. Established relationships among agricultural partners and stakeholders create opportunities to collaborate in proactive, voluntary, and community-based solutions to meet the world's increasing food demands while conserving SGCN. Collaboratively enhancing and incentivizing these partnerships into the future will be necessary for sustaining Idaho's SGCN, vital agricultural-based economy, and community culture and heritage.

figure.figDesc: In 2019, renewable sources generated 76% of in-state electricity with hydroelectricity composing 58%(OEMR 2022). Construction of new utility-scale wind and solar energy facilities is increasing in Idaho to reduce carbon-based electricity generation, which is a goal of the state's electric utilities. First constructed in 2006, Idaho's utility-scale wind energy facilities now provide 16% of in-state generation. More than an estimated 200,000 megawatts of wind energy remain available for development

note.p: ). Idaho's electricity generation is primarily from renewable energy sources that include hydroelectricity, wind, solar, geothermal, and biomass

figure.figDesc: • Mining-Global mineral demands are prompting new exploration and industrial-scale mining in Idaho. Idaho has an extensive mining history dating back to the mid-1800s. Gold was the key mineral that originally attracted prospectors to Idaho. Now, silver and phosphate are the most commonly produced minerals with Idaho supplying about 45% and 22% of the nation's silver and phosphate, respectively. Idaho produces many other valuable minerals including antimony, tungsten, cobalt, vanadium, molybdenum, and gemstones. Quarrying of sand, gravel, and crushed rock provides crucial raw materials for the construction sector and transportation system, which are expanding in response to Idaho's growing human population.County, state, and federal regulatory authorities hold much of Idaho's lands and waters supplying energy and mineral resources in public trust. These same lands and waters also support fish, wildlife, and plants, including SGCN. Utility-scale energy production and industrial-scale mining projects usually have long-term life cycles of construction, operations, reclamation, and restoration, which can affect SGCN conservation for decades. For example, legacy effects of mining in the 19th and 20th centuries continue to impair the health and productivity of some Idaho lands and waters, including SGCN habitats. Today, responsible siting and BMPs can help Energy Production & Mining projects reduce negative effects on SGCN.

Energy Production & Mining's products and services can be compatible with SGCN conservation when stakeholders collaborate. Many long-standing partners associated with Energy Production & Mining are already contributing in many ways to conserving the state's fish, wildlife, and plants. In addition to licensing and permitting, established relationships among Energy Production & Mining partners and stakeholders create opportunities to collaborate in proactive, voluntary, and community-oriented solutions to meet society's needs while conserving SGCN. Considering the increasing local and global energy and mineral needs, collaboratively enhancing and incentivizing these partnerships into the future will be necessary for sustaining Idaho's SGCN, modern society, economies, and communities.

figure.head: Voluntary Actions Related to Native Species and Their Habitats •

The following are examples of voluntary actions: o Participate in land-use and resource planning processes, communicate the state's SGCN goals and objectives, identify potential risks to SGCN goals and objectives from future energy and mineral development, and recommend measures to address risks. o Develop, assemble, maintain, and disseminate databases to support land-use and project planning. o Identify and address SGCN knowledge gaps and proactively develop information to support project planning, effects analysis, and measures to offset negative effects. , operations, and maintenance BMPs; and human activity and noise reduction) (e.g., IDAPA 20.03.02.140; EPA 2012; Jones 2012; REWI 2023). o Incentivize project proponents to conserve SGCN and their habitats. o Protect sensitive or vulnerable animal and plant SGCN populations and their habitats. o Construct or upgrade facilities and infrastructure to benefit fish and wildlife movements. o Avoid, minimize, and compensate for negative effects on SGCN from facilities, infrastructure, operations, and maintenance (e.g., bird detection/turbine curtailment technologies and bat deterrent technologies at wind energy facilities and capping pipes marking mining claims). o Manage vegetation associated with energy and mining projects to minimize negative effects on SGCN and maximize beneficial effects (e.g., pollinatorfriendly vegetation management). o Implement Integrated Pest Management principles to reduce the introduction and spread of invasive species while benefiting pollinator habitat (ISDA 2016; WAFWA 2019; USDA 2021; IISC 2022; USDA 2022). o Construct new power lines according to the Avian Power Line Interaction Committee (APLIC) protocols to protect bird SGCN from electrocution and collisions.

In addition to Overarching Effects & Actions, the following subsections identify potential effects of stressors on key SGCN habitat and propose collaborative actions to offset negative effects if they occur. Key habitats were identified and prioritized for actions based on the estimated feasibility and effectiveness to address challenge-specific stressors likely to affect SGCN during the next 10 years. Chapter 2 habitats form the organization of the following subsections. Voluntary actions apply to key habitats with the potential for negative SGCN effects from stressors associated with Energy Production & Mining. Ideally, SGCN conservation will be mutually beneficial for responsible Energy Production & Mining. Mining projects have the potential to affect Forest & Woodland habitats, where mineral resources are relatively abundant. Increasing global demands for minerals have increased mining project proposals across Idaho. Idaho's forests also support local forestry and ranching economies and provide abundant opportunities for outdoor recreation. Consequently, Energy Production & Mining projects can change existing land uses and potentially reduce SGCN habitat; project infrastructure and activities can influence SGCN behavior (e.g., avoidance, displacement, or movement patterns). In addition to Energy Production & Mining, other stressors potentially affecting Forest & Woodland habitats include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, urban development, the introduction and spread of invasive species, and unnatural wildfire frequency, extent, and severity. These interacting stressors can further affect both SGCN habitat and important amenities that Forest & Woodland habitats provide to Idaho communities. Examples of SGCN occurring in Forest & Woodland habitats and potentially influenced by Energy Production & Mining include Fisher, Grizzly Bear, Moose, Lewis's Woodpecker, Whiteheaded Woodpecker, Olive-sided Flycatcher, Cassin's Finch, Western Bumble Bee, Gillette's Checkerspot, and Clearwater Phlox. Proposed voluntary actions intended to address the negative effects of stressors if occurring, and thus benefit SGCN conservation and responsible Energy Production & Mining projects, are listed in Table 3.3.1. figure.figDesc: 3.1 Voluntary actions intended to benefit SGCN and responsible Energy Production & Mining if stressors are affecting the quantity, quality, or connectivity of Forest & Woodland habitats (continued) Energy Production & Mining infrastructure and activities have the potential to affect Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats. Water is often necessary for energy and mineral projects. Therefore, the use of surface water and groundwater and the release of water pollutants through industrial facilities and stormwater discharges can also potentially affect Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats. Additional stressors potentially affecting Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, shifting seasonal water runoff patterns, and the introduction and spread of invasive species. These interacting stressors can further affect both SGCN habitat and important amenities that Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats provide to Idaho communities. Depending on circumstances, IDWR and USACE might regulate energy and mineral projects in Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats per the ISCPA and CWA, respectively (IDWR 2022b). Therefore, facilities and infrastructure associated with energy and mineral projects in wetlands and riparian zones might need state and federal permits that could include protective measures for SGCN. Examples of SGCN occurring in Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats and potentially influenced by Energy Production & Mining include Northern Leopard Frog, Hoary Bat, Silver-haired Bat, Moose, Trumpeter Swan, Sandhill Crane, White-faced Ibis, Short-eared Owl, Western Bumble Bee, Monarch Butterfly, Water Howellia, and Ute Ladies-tresses. figure.figDesc: Renewable energy and mineral resources are relatively abundant in Idaho's expansive Desert & Semidesert habitats. Therefore, proposals for renewable energy and mining projects are increasing, particularly across southern Idaho. These areas also support traditional local economies including ranching and outdoor recreation. Consequently, Energy Production & Mining projects in Desert & Semidesert habitats can change existing land uses and potentially reduce SGCN habitat. In addition to changing land uses, other stressors potentially affecting Desert & Semidesert habitats include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, urban development, the introduction and spread of invasive species, and unnatural wildfire frequency, extent, and severity. Examples of SGCN occurring in Desert & Semidesert habitats and potentially influenced by Energy Production & Mining include Woodhouse's Toad, Pygmy Rabbit, Pronghorn, California Bighorn Sheep, Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep, Greater Sage-Grouse, Long-billed Curlew, Golden Eagle, Short-eared Owl, Sagebrush Sparrow, Yellow Bumble Bee, Morrison Bumble Bee, Slickspot Peppergrass, and Spalding's Catchfly. figure.figDesc: 3.3 Voluntary actions intended to benefit SGCN and responsible Energy Production & Mining if stressors are affecting the quantity, quality, or connectivity of Desert & Semidesert habitats (continued) Energy Production & Mining has the potential to affect Aquatic Vegetation & Freshwater Habitat (hereafter aquatic habitat) by using surface water and groundwater and releasing water pollutants through industrial facilities and stormwater discharges. In addition to Energy Production & Mining, other stressors potentially affecting aquatic habitat include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, shifting seasonal water runoff patterns, other pollutant sources decreasing water quality, and the introduction and spread of invasive species. Idaho's water allocation and distribution processes administered by IDWR regulate the diversion of public waters for Energy Production & Mining. State and federal permitting also regulate pollutant discharges to public waters from Energy Production & Mining facilities including IPDES administered by DEQ(DEQ 2022b) and NPDES administered by EPA(EPA 2022b) under the CWA(EPA 2022a). IDPES and NPDES permits include measures to meet water quality standards. In addition, water conservation programs and BMPs can further improve Energy Production & Mining operational efficiencies thereby reducing water diversions and pollutants(DEQ 2022a). Examples of SGCN occurring in aquatic habitat and potentially influenced by Energy Production & Mining include White Sturgeon, Yellowstone Cutthroat Trout, Bonneville Cutthroat Trout, steelhead, Sockeye Salmon, Chinook Salmon, Mountain Whitefish, Bull Trout, Moose, Harlequin Duck, Western Grebe, and Ring-billed Gull. The lands and waters that Transportation & Service Corridors occupy and cross support many important fish, wildlife, and plants, including SGCN. Therefore, stressors associated with Transportation & Service Corridors can inadvertently have long-term effects on SGCN. These interacting stressors can further affect both SGCN habitat and important amenities that Forest & Woodland habitats provide to Idaho communities. Table 3.4.1 Voluntary actions intended to benefit SGCN and responsible Transportation & Service Corridors if stressors are affecting the quantity, quality, or connectivity of Forest & Woodland habitatsThe construction and maintenance of infrastructure associated with Transportation & Service Corridors have the potential to affect Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats. Additional stressors potentially affecting Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, shifting seasonal water runoff patterns, water pollutants, and the introduction and spread of invasive species. These interacting stressors can further affect both SGCN habitat and important amenities that Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats provide to Idaho communities. Depending on circumstances, IDWR and USACE might regulate infrastructure construction and maintenance in Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats per the ISCPA and CWA, respectively (IDWR 2022b). Therefore, infrastructure associated with Transportation & Service Corridors in wetlands and riparian zones might need state and federal permits that could include protective measures for SGCN. Transportation & Service Corridors and related construction and maintenance activities have the potential to affect Desert & Semidesert habitats. Road densities and traffic can also result in wildlife-vehicle collisions and influence SGCN behavior (e.g., avoidance, displacement, and movement patterns). In addition to Transportation & Service Corridors, other stressors potentially affecting Desert & Semidesert habitats include prolonged drought, decreased snowpack, natural resource development, the introduction and spread of invasive species, and unnatural wildfire frequency, extent, and severity. These interacting stressors can further affect both SGCN habitat and important amenities that Desert & Semidesert habitat provides to Idaho communities. For example, invasive plants often spread along Transportation & Service Corridors. Elevated risks of wildfire ignition can also be associated with Transportation & Service Corridors (Shinneman et al. 2018).

row.cell: hunting, fishing & trapping," which is managed by IDFG under the supervision of the Idaho Fish
Forestry includes public and private forest management and infrastructure, timber harvest,
and forest product manufacturing. Idaho's public and private forests and waters provide
society with abundant renewable resources and services including forest products (e.g., wood,
paper, and furniture), livestock forage, healthy soils, clean air and water, erosion and flood
control, and outdoor recreational opportunities. Forests also provide important habitat for fish,
wildlife, and plants, including SGCN. The forest industry also contributes importantly to Idaho's
economy, local communities, and way of life. For example, managing Idaho's 16.5 million acres
(6.7 million ha) of forests available for harvesting forest products employs approximately
3,250 people. In 2020, forestry contributed $2.4 billion to the state's economy and supported
over 31,000 jobs (Idaho Forest Products Commission 2020). Demand for forest products is
increasing as the human population increases globally, nationally, and locally.

Fig. 3.4.2 Moose using newly developed passage opportunity under Idaho State Highway 28 IDFG.3.5 Biological Resource UseOverview Biological Resource Use consists of Hunting & Collecting Terrestrial Animals, Logging & Wood Harvesting, and Fishing & Harvesting Aquatic Resources (CMP 2016a). Logging & Wood Harvesting is referenced here as "forestry," to more holistically address the manufacturing of forest products and forest management. Similarly, Hunting & Collecting Terrestrial Animals and Fishing & Harvesting Aquatic Resources are referenced here collectively as "recreational Forestry's production of renewable products and services for society can be compatible with SGCN conservation when stakeholders collaborate in problem solving. The WGA Policy Resolution 2021-03, National Forest and Rangeland Management (WGA 2021a), emphasizes the importance of collaboration and strategic planning between stakeholders to achieve healthy forests. Many long-standing partners associated with forestry are already contributing greatly to conserving the state's fish, wildlife, and plants. Established relationships among forestry partners and stakeholders can create opportunities to collaborate in proactive, voluntary, and community-based solutions to meet society's needs while conserving SGCN.

figure.figDesc: Additional stressors potentially affecting Forest & Woodland habitats include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, shifting seasonal water runoff patterns, disease and insect outbreaks, the introduction and spread of invasive species, and unnatural wildfire frequency, extent, and severity. These interacting stressors can further affect SGCN habitat, forest health, and important forestry products and services for society(Dale et al. 2001;Hessburg et al. 2022). For example, fire is an important stressor that can benefit some forests when carefully managed. However, stressors that elevate the risk of unnatural wildfire can create severe consequences for the sustainability of forestry and communities, especially along expanding WUIs.

figure.figDesc: -based military training ranges including the US Air Force's special use airspace, associated with Mountain Home Air Force Base, and Idaho Army National Guard's Orchard Combat Training Center, both in southwest Idaho.The military is important to Idaho's economy, communities, and culture. However, Military Exercises and installations have the potential to affect SGCN. The Department of Defense (DOD) manages natural resources associated with military installations, including SGCN, through Integrated Natural Resources Management Plans (INRMPs). The DOD also addresses effects of Military Exercises on natural resources through NEPA processes. The State of Idaho routinely participates in the DOD's INRMP and NEPA processes to identify and address effects on priority wildlife and plants. The state will continue to collaborate with the DOD as an important partner for conserving Idaho's SGCN while supporting the nation's military.

Establish collaborative working groups as appropriate including communities, industries, regulatory authorities, and resource managers to facilitate the exchange of information and knowledge about opportunities and efforts to benefit SGCN, assist DOD, and support communities. • Participate with DOD, resource managers, and other stakeholders to develop collaborative measures to offset negative effects of Military Exercises on SGCN. • Prepare and disseminate information, education, and outreach materials informing stakeholders about opportunities to incorporate SGCN conservation into Military Exercises. • Encourage public and stakeholder participation in INRMP and NEPA processes to raise awareness and consideration of both SGCN conservation needs and Military Exercise needs. • Encourage data sharing to support proactive and adaptive management for SGCN conservation. In addition to Overarching Effects & Actions, the following subsections identify potential effects of stressors on key SGCN habitats and propose collaborative actions to offset negative effects if they occur. Key habitats were identified and prioritized for actions based on the estimated feasibility and effectiveness to address challenge-specific stressors likely to affect SGCN during the next 10 years. Habitats in Chapter 2 form the organization of the following subsections. Voluntary actions apply to key habitats with the potential for negative SGCN effects from stressors associated with outdoor recreation. Ideally, SGCN conservation will be mutually beneficial for outdoor recreation. Camping, hiking, biking, OHV touring, horseback riding, sightseeing, wildlife viewing, and hunting are popular forms of outdoor recreation in Forest & Woodland habitats. However, outdoor recreation activities, facilities, and infrastructure also have the potential to locally affect Forest & Woodland habitats. For example, outdoor recreation activities and infrastructure can disturb or displace wildlife, remove vegetation, spread invasive species, cause erosion, and compact soils. Additional stressors potentially affecting Forest & Woodland habitats more broadly include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, insect and disease outbreaks, the introduction and spread of invasive species, and unnatural wildfire frequency, extent, and severity. Outdoor recreation can worsen these stressors by spreading invasive plants and elevating ignition risks for unnatural wildfire, which can negatively affect SGCN, forest health, and recreational opportunities for Idaho communities. Examples of SGCN occurring in Forest & Woodland habitats and potentially influenced by outdoor recreation include Wolverine, Fisher, Rocky Mountain Goat, Moose, Yellow-billed Cuckoo, Lewis's Woodpecker, Pinyon Jay, Clark's Nutcracker, Cassia Crossbill, Western Bumble Bee, Whitebark Pine, and Indian Valley Sedge. Proposed voluntary actions intended to address the negative effects of stressors if occurring, and thus benefit SGCN conservation and outdoor recreation, are listed in Table 3.6.1.

figure.figDesc: 6.2 Voluntary actions intended to benefit SGCN and sustainable outdoor recreation if stressors are affecting the quantity, quality, or connectivity of Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats Much of Idaho's Desert & Semidesert habitats occurs on public lands administered by the BLM and FS. These public lands provide abundant open spaces and opportunities for outdoor recreation. Camping, hiking, biking, OHV touring, horseback riding, sightseeing, rock hounding, wildlife viewing, and hunting are popular forms of outdoor recreation in Desert & Semidesert habitats. However, outdoor recreation activities, facilities, and infrastructure also have the potential to locally affect Desert & Semidesert habitats. For example, outdoor recreation activities and infrastructure can locally disturb or displace wildlife, remove vegetation, cause erosion, and compact soils. Additional stressors potentially affecting Desert & Semidesert habitats more broadly include prolonged drought, decreased snowpack, natural resource development, the introduction and spread of invasive species, and unnatural wildfire frequency, extent, and severity. These interacting stressors can further affect SGCN habitat, rangeland health, and outdoor recreation provided to Idaho communities. For example, the increasing prevalence of invasive plants and unnatural destructive wildfire are harmful stressors affecting Desert & Semidesert habitats (Chambers et al. 2014; Chambers et al. 2019). Outdoor recreation can potentially worsen these stressors by spreading invasive plants and elevating wildfire ignition risks. Examples of SGCN occurring in Desert & Semidesert habitats and potentially influenced by outdoor recreation include Woodhouse's Toad, Pygmy Rabbit, Pronghorn, California Bighorn Sheep, Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep, Greater Sage-Grouse, Long-billed Curlew, Golden Eagle, Burrowing Owl, Sagebrush Sparrow, Yellow Bumble Bee, Morrison Bumble Bee, Slickspot Peppergrass, and Winward's Goldenbrush. Therefore, prescribed burning is a key tool for collaborative forest and rangeland health initiatives.The values and goals of wildland fire management are typically compatible with SGCN conservation, especially when stakeholders collaborate in community-minded solutions(Bothwell 2019).WGA Policy Resolution 2021-03, National Forest and Rangeland Management (WGA 2021a), emphasizes the importance of collaborative fire management planning and project implementation for healthy forests and rangelands across federal, state, and private ownerships. Many long-standing partners associated with fire management are already contributing in many ways to conserving the state's fish, wildlife, and plants. Established relationships between fire management partners and stakeholders can create opportunities to collaborate in proactive, voluntary, and community-based solutions to meet society's needs while conserving SGCN. Considering the increasing risks of destructive wildfire, collaboratively enhancing and incentivizing these partnerships into the future will be necessary for sustaining Idaho's SGCN, natural resource-based economy, and communities.

figure.figDesc: Temperate & Boreal Grassland & Shrubland habitats have been significantly affected by invasive plants such as Cheatgrass, North Africa Grass, Yellow Star-thistle, Rush Skeletonweed, and Medusahead. These invasive plants reduce rangeland health and productivity by outcompeting desirable native plants. The unnatural fuel loads from these invasive plants are also increasing the frequency, size, and intensity of destructive wildfires. Conversely, wildfire suppression in some grasslands has contributed to invasions by conifer trees. Other stressors potentially affecting Temperate & Boreal Grassland & Shrubland habitats include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, and shifting seasonal water runoff patterns. These interacting stressors can further affect SGCN habitat, rangeland health, and important goods and services that Temperate & Boreal Grassland & Shrubland habitats provide to Idaho communities. Examples of SGCN occurring in Temperate & Boreal Grassland & Shrubland habitats and potentially influenced by fire management include American Pika, Northern Idaho Ground Squirrel, Southern Idaho Ground Squirrel, Rocky Mountain Goat, California Bighorn Sheep, Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep, Mountain Quail, Sharp-tailed Grouse, Long-billed Curlew, Grasshopper Sparrow, Yellow Bumble Bee, Western Bumble Bee, Monarch Butterfly, and Spalding's Catchfly. figure.figDesc: Undesirable invasive plants (e.g., Cheatgrass, North Africa Grass, Yellow Star-thistle, Rush Skeletonweed, and Medusahead) harm the health of Temperate & Boreal Grassland & Shrubland habitats. These invasive plants reduce rangeland health and productivity by outcompeting desirable native plants. The unnatural fuel loads from invasive plants are also increasing the frequency, size, and intensity of wildfires. These invasive plants also negatively affect SGCN habitat. Additional stressors potentially affecting Temperate & Boreal Grassland & Shrubland habitats include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, shifting seasonal water runoff patterns, and unnatural wildfire frequency, extent, and severity. These interacting stressors can further affect SGCN habitat, rangeland health, and important products and services that Temperate & Boreal Grassland & Shrubland habitats provide to Idaho communities. Examples of SGCN occurring in Temperate & Boreal Grassland & Shrubland habitats and potentially influenced by invasive species include American Pika, Northern Idaho Ground Squirrel, Rocky Mountain Goat, California Bighorn Sheep, Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep, Mountain Quail, Sharp-tailed Grouse, Long-billed Curlew, Western Bumble Bee, Monarch Butterfly, and Spalding's Catchfly. Proposed voluntary actions intended to address the negative effects of stressors if occurring, and thus benefit SGCN conservation and rangeland health, are listed in Table 3.8.2.Table 3.8.2 Voluntary actions intended to benefit SGCN and invasive species management if stressors are affecting the quantity, quality, or connectivity of Temperate & Boreal Grassland & Shrubland habitats Undesirable invasive plants (e.g., Purple Loosestrife and Common Reed) harm the health of Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats. Invasive plants can reduce wetland and riparian health and productivity by outcompeting desirable native plants, reducing the diversity of plant species, forming exceptionally dense stands, and interrupting water flow patterns. In addition, invasive nonnative wildlife can outcompete or prey upon native species. For example, competition and predation by the American Bullfrog can also compound negative effects of an invasive fungal disease (i.e., Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis [Bd]) on native amphibians. Consequently, invasive species can impair the health of wetland and riparian habitats. Additional stressors potentially affecting Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, shifting seasonal water runoff patterns, and pollutants decreasing water quality. These interacting stressors can further affect SGCN habitat and important amenities provided to Idaho communities. Examples of SGCN occurring in Shrub & Herb Wetland habitats and potentially influenced by invasive species include Northern Leopard Frog, Little Brown Myotis, Hoary Bat, Silver-haired Bat, Moose, Trumpeter Swan, Northern Pintail, Sandhill Crane, White-faced Ibis, Short-eared Owl, Western Bumble Bee, Monarch Butterfly, Water Howellia, and Ute Ladies-tresses. figure.figDesc: 11.1 Voluntary actions intended to benefit SGCN and address climate-related stressors if affecting the quantity, quality, or connectivity of Forest & Woodland habitats (continued)Warmer temperatures, wetter springs, drier summers, and earlier snowmelt are causing more frequent, severe, and longer lasting droughts. These droughts harm the health and productivity of Montane-Foothill Grassland & Shrubland habitats by decreasing soil moisture, increasing invasive species infestations, and increasing destructive wildfire. Consequently, some grasslands and shrublands are shrinking, mainly in low-elevation dry sites, and expanding in areas now with longer growing seasons. Some SGCN associated with grasslands and shrublands might shift their ranges with changing habitat distributions. However, other SGCN on small and isolated remnants, like Palouse Prairie grasslands, are unlikely to adapt.

Polar & High Montane Scrub, Grassland & Barrens
Polar & High Montane Scrub, Grassland & Barrens habitat (hereafter Alpine Tundra) is diverse
and influenced by localized and small-scale changes in snow, wind, and soil moisture, which

figure.head: Idaho Department of Fish & Game 275 also
figure.figDesc: change with aspect, slope, and elevation. This diverse habitat can support a diversity of SGCN. In some cases, topographic variability can help moderate negative effects of climaterelated stressors. However, Alpine Tundra is expected overall to shrink from warming temperatures, longer growing seasons, less snowpack, and more precipitation as rain. These stressors can also cause more soil erosion and higher risks of unnatural wildfire.Examples of SGCN occurring in Alpine Tundra and potentially influenced by climate-related stressors include American Pika, Wolverine, Grizzly Bear, Rocky Mountain Goat, Golden Eagle, Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch, and Black Rosy-Finch. figure.figDesc: These stressors can also decrease crop yields and rangeland forage. To adapt to a warmer and drier climate, many agricultural producers and resource managers may need to adopt new practices including choices about drought-and disease-tolerant crops and livestock breeds, irrigation efficiencies, and changing livestock management practices. Eventually, agricultural producers may be faced with decisions about additional costs of adapting to climate-related stressors and remaining profitable. High property values compared to agricultural commodity prices is already a driver for urbanizing agricultural lands. For example, 11 million acres (4.5 million ha) of US agricultural lands were converted to nonagricultural uses between 2001 and 2016(Freedgood et al. 2020). Therefore, collaboratively protecting lands and waters can be mutually beneficial for Idaho's SGCN conservation, agricultural economy, and rural communities.Examples of SGCN occurring in Agricultural Habitat and potentially influenced by climaterelated stressors include Little Brown Myotis, Hoary Bat, Silver-haired Bat, Pronghorn, Moose, Franklin's Gull, White-faced Ibis, Bobolink, Western Bumble Bee, and Monarch Butterfly. Overarching and interrelated climate-related stressors affecting Aquatic Vegetation & Freshwater Habitat (hereafter aquatic habitat) include warming temperatures, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, shifting seasonal water runoff patterns, prolonged and severe drought, pollutants decreasing water quality, changing wind patterns, and extreme weather events such as flooding. Drought and warming water also harm water quality, which can increase invasive species and harmful algal blooms (Fig.3.11.4). note.p: OverviewWith more than 8,000 species (vertebrates, invertebrates, and plants) native to Idaho, even basic information about distribution, abundance, or habitat requirements can understandably be lacking for many species. Unfortunately, a lack of basic information can prevent proper ver.2024-01-16 Idaho Department of Fish & Game 284

figure.head: Idaho Department of Fish & Game 285 been
figure.figDesc: documented downriver in Kootenay Lake, BC. Idaho specimens may therefore be misidentified as Peamouth Chub, which are common in the Kootenai River. Alternatively, Lake Chub might seasonally move from Kootenay Lake in BC upriver into the Kootenai River in Idaho.• Nevada Goldenrod-This species is ranked SH and the only known Idaho collection is from Owyhee County in 1964. The priority action for this species is to search the vicinity of the Idaho collection, as well as an Oregon collection, which is just west of the state line in Malheur County.

Northern Bog Lemming-Under review for ESA protection as of this writing, the species' distribution is Idaho is known from 23 observations (most recently detected in 2003) in Bonner and Boundary Counties. Idaho represents the southern extent of the species' distribution and more intensive and extensive surveys over a wide range of habitats are needed to determine distribution accurately. The lack of understanding is in part due to difficulties in surveying for the species, and newer survey methods are being tested with Montana and Washington partners (e.g., DNA of fecal pellets and eDNA).

figure.figDesc: • Long-eared Myotis, Long-legged Myotis, and Big Brown Bat-In June 2022, the fungus Pd that causes WNS was detected in Minnetonka Cave in southeast Idaho. These 3 bat species are known to be vulnerable to the disease and have experienced related population declines in other states. Additional information on disease prevalence and population trends is needed, because Long-legged Myotis tested positive for Pd and all 3 species are known to hibernate in Minnetonka Cave.• American White Pelican-IDFG manages this species per the commission-approved Management Plan for the Conservation of American White Pelicans inIdaho 2016Idaho -2025

Pygmy Whitefish-This fish SGIN is known to occur only in 5 narrow and deep lakes: Upper Priest, Priest, Pend Oreille, Spirit, and Hayden. Although appearing to be relatively common in some lakes, current population data are insufficient to estimate trends.• Wyoming Ground Squirrel (ssp. nevadensis)-This subspecies is limited to arid southwest Idaho and thought to be declining, but to an unknown degree. No Wyoming Ground Squirrel surveys have occurred since the 1980s. • Boreal Owl and American Pipit-These 2 species occur in restricted alpine and subalpine habitats potentially affected by a loss of snowpack and changing seasonal runoff patterns. Both species are suspected to be declining, but current monitoring data are insufficient to estimate reliable trends. Breeding populations of the American Pipit may be especially limited and becoming more so with tree line advancement. • Evening Grosbeak-Given the steady, continent-wide declines of this SGIN, better understanding relationships with, and the status of, key associated habitats (notably Dry Lower Montane-Foothill Forest, Mesic Lower Montane Forest, and Aspen Forest & Woodland) will be important.

figure.figDesc: on whether or not to invest in monitoring, and what type of monitoring to take to improve management (Fig.4.2). We plan to use this framework as a means to evaluate monitoring in the context of financial limitations and the urgency of conservation problems.It is important to select M&E indicators that allow us to measure progress toward our objectives. A good indicator should be both representative and measurable. The Conservation Measures Partnership's (CMP) Conservation Standards(CMP 2020) provides additional advice on what constitutes good indicators. We plan to give considerable thought to what indicators will be most relevant and useful to our objectives. In most cases, the selection of indicators will be influenced by the cost-effectiveness of employing a particular indicator, the availability of existing data, its sensitivity to the action being taken, and how consistently it is defined and used. The availability of existing data is often a crucial factor because the need to gather new data can sometimes be too expensive.The report Measuring the Effectiveness of State Wildlife Grants(AFWA 2011) describes a framework that states and their partners can use to assess the effectiveness of conservation actions. This framework includes a list of common or generic conservation actions and a process for developing results, objectives, effectiveness measures (indicators), and data collection questionnaires. Identifying effectiveness measures for SWAPs not only improves conservation work, but also helps demonstrate to policy makers that the STWG program is leading to the outcomes intended by Congress and therefore is a good investment of public funds. We plan to use this report to inform our effectiveness measures.
