figure.head: Idaho Department of Fish & Game 300 Conservation Success Story: SOUTHERN IDAHO GROUND SQUIRREL Southern
figure.figDesc: Idaho Ground Squirrels are found in lower-elevation, shrub-steppe habitat of the lower Weiser and Payette river basins and are native to only 4 Counties (Adams, Gem, Payette, and Washington) in southwest Idaho. The FWS was petitioned to list the species under the ESA in 2001, and that same year, IDFG began a 5-year survey in collaboration with the College of Idaho to better document Southern Idaho Ground Squirrel distribution and abundance. In addition, a Candidate Conservation Agreement with Assurances (CCAA) encompassing almost 10% of the squirrel's known range was completed between the State of Idaho, private landowners, and FWS.Surveys generated distribution and abundance information showing that the Southern Idaho Ground Squirrel existed throughout most of its historical range and populations appeared stable.

figure.head: Idaho Department of Fish & Game 301 Conservation Success Story: WOLVERINE In
figure.figDesc: 2015, IDFG partnered with a diverse group including neighboring state fish and wildlife agencies, federal, tribal, university, and NGOs on a vast project using motion-triggered cameras to establish a baseline of Wolverine distribution across the western US.

figure.head: Idaho Department of Fish & Game 302 Conservation Success Story: BONNEVILLE CUTTHROAT TROUT Within
figure.figDesc: the Idaho portion of their range, Bonneville Cutthroat Trout are exclusively found within the Bear River drainage in southeastern Idaho. Historic population declines caused by irrigation for agriculture, hydropower, grazing, overfishing, and competition from introduced fish species, such as Brook Trout, led biologists in the 1950s to mistakenly believe the species had been extirpated from the state.Federal, state, and tribal wildlife agencies, along with NGOs such as Trout Unlimited and Western Native Trout Initiative worked for decades to implement a multitude of conservation and restoration projects to benefit Bonneville Cutthroat Trout.

note.p: Regardless of this latest decision, IDFG continues to lead in providing the best available science to inform the conservation of this species by repeating and expanding the multistate camera survey on a regular basis, participating in US-Canada population genetics work, and supporting additional research on the relationship between Wolverine behavior and winter recreation. The Management Plan for the Conservation of Wolverines in Idaho 2014-2019(IDFG 2014), prepared primarily to lead state efforts to maintain viable populations of Wolverines in Idaho, has recently been updated and incorporated into the Management Plan for theConservation of Fisher, Wolverine, and Canada Lynx in Idaho 2023-2028 (IDFG 2023b).

div.head: Aquatic Vegetation & Freshwater Habitat
div.p: The construction and maintenance of infrastructure for Transportation & Service Corridors have the potential to affect Aquatic Vegetation & Freshwater Habitat (hereafter aquatic habitat). Other potential stressors affecting aquatic habitat include prolonged drought, changing precipitation and snowpack trends, shifting seasonal water runoff patterns, pollutants decreasing water quality, and the introduction and spread of invasive species. These interacting stressors can further affect SGCN habitat, important amenities that aquatic habitat provides to Idaho communities, and cause risks to Transportation & Service Corridors investments (Gillespie et al. 2014). For example, the design, construction, and maintenance of highway bridges and pipelines crossing rivers can be more difficult with unpredictable precipitation and seasonal runoff patterns. Manage aquatic habitat to benefit SGCN and conserve water supplies and water quality (e.g., construction and maintenance BMPs, stormwater management, pollution prevention and control, erosion prevention and control, vegetated buffers, and road-salt reduction) (e.g., EPA 2009;DEQ 2020;FWS 2022;EPA 2023b).
ver. 2024-01-16 Idaho Department of Fish & Game 212 Water quality is reduced by soil erosion, increased sediment inputs, and pollutants.

Conserve water supplies and water quality (e.g., buffers/setbacks, vegetated buffers, improved stormwater management, upgraded water treatment facilities, waste disposal and management facilities, recreational infrastructure and facility maintenance, and information and education).

Provide technical assistance during water-related regulatory processes (e.g., diversion rates, water levels and streamflow, aquifer recharge, in-water work windows, fish passage, flood-resilient infrastructure siting, buffers/setbacks, habitat restoration, mitigation, and invasive species). Examples of SGCN occurring in Caves & Subterranean Habitats (including abandoned mines) and potentially affected by outdoor recreation include Western Small-footed Myotis, Little Brown Myotis, Yuma Myotis, Silver-haired Bat, and Townsend's Big-eared Bat (also see Sections 3.11 and 3.12). Proposed voluntary actions intended to address the negative effects of stressors if occurring, and thus benefit SGCN conservation and outdoor recreation, are listed in Table 3.6.6. SGCN survival decreases from the introduction of harmful diseases.

Assist the outdoor recreation industry, cave tourism businesses, recreationists, and resource managers with conserving subterranean habitat as appropriate to benefit SGCN, the outdoor recreation economy, and communities.

Manage subterranean habitat to benefit SGCN and outdoor recreation (e.g., access management, batcompatible gates in abandoned mine openings, airflow maintenance, invasive species control, and information and education).

div.head: Idaho Department of Fish & Game 296
div.p: The purchase of the conservation lease not only protected a key Columbia Spotted Frog population; it also allowed livestock grazing to continue on adjacent lands benefiting both wildlife and people on working lands.

div.head: Conservation Success Story: GREATER SAGE-GROUSE
div.p: After numerous petitions, the FWS determined that Greater Sage-Grouse warranted protection under the ESA based on habitat loss and inadequate regulatory mechanisms. In 2012, then-Governor Butch Otter convened Idaho's "Sage-Grouse Task Force" to develop an Idaho-specific sage-grouse conservation plan and address shortcomings outlined in the ESA listing petitions.

IDFG partnered with state and federal agencies to incorporate the updated conservation strategy into BLM and FS management plans. The state continued to collaborate with federal agencies to develop solutions for sage-grouse conservation in Idaho, which culminated in the 2015 final plan for sage-grouse conservation on federal lands. Due in part to these efforts, the FWS in 2015 concluded that the sage-grouse did not require protections under the ESA, and Idaho retained full management authority for this iconic western bird.

By retaining state control, Idaho avoided potentially negative impacts to the many land-based industries across southern Idaho, such as livestock grazing, agriculture, and energy development. Greater Sage-Grouse also remains a favorite upland game bird that hunters enjoy pursuing each fall during a carefully managed hunting season. SWAP funding helped organize and implement a multiyear, multiorganization effort to better understand the habitat needs of Fishers in north-central Idaho. Prior to this, Fisher conservation had received little attention, and the animal's low population densities and association with mature, unlogged forests led many to believe future petitions for listing under the ESA were likely.

To address the knowledge gap of Fisher conservation and habitat use, IDFG initiated a project to learn more about the species' distribution and habitat requirements. DNA hair snaring and satellite radio collars were used to collect occurrence and movement data, and that information was used to show Fisher distribution and habitat preferences.

The effort provided valuable new information about Fishers and their habitat and distribution in Idaho that contributed to the FWS deciding that an ESA listing was not needed. Idaho retained management authority for the species and helped preserve timber-based jobs to the benefit of local economies in north-central Idaho.

Gaining a better understanding of this species by using best available science not only produced more knowledge about its habitat requirements; it also helped forest managers better understand the Fisher's needs and take that into consideration when planning forest management projects. Surveys were conducted to determine Pygmy Rabbit occurrence, and genetic studies were conducted to validate the species' presence based on analysis of fecal pellet samples. In general, Pygmy Rabbits in Idaho were found to be more widespread and populations better connected than previously thought.

This information directly contributed to the 2010 decision by the FWS to not list the rabbit under the ESA, thereby avoiding unnecessary federal oversight that could have negatively impacted land-based economies across southern and eastern Idaho, such as livestock grazing, agricultural production, and energy development.

Continuing sagebrush habitat work across southern Idaho benefits Pygmy Rabbits, as well as Greater Sage-Grouse, Mule Deer, Slickspot Peppergrass and other important plant and animal species that rely on this habitat. that could not be cropped without improvements. In other areas, it is barely able to be grazed and is only marginally better than wasteland.

phylogeny:
div.p: The origin of groups. Phylogenetic trees are diagrams that depict the origin and evolution of groups of organisms.

population: A group of organisms of the same species occupying a particular space at a particular time, with the potential to breed with each other. For the purpose of determining practical conservation value, we interpret "group" to mean two or more individuals.

rangeland: Land on which the indigenous vegetation (climax or natural potential) is predominantly grasses, grass-like plants, forbs, or shrubs and is managed as a natural ecosystem. If plants are introduced, they are managed similarly. Rangeland includes natural grasslands, savannas, shrublands, many deserts, tundra, alpine communities, marshes, and meadows.

div.head: recruitment:
div.p: The increase in a natural population as offspring grow and immigrants arrive.

regional endemic: Species endemic to a particular geographic region (e.g., Pacific Northwest, Great Basin, Columbia Plateau, Rocky Mountains), but not restricted to Idaho. For our purposes, this includes species whose distribution includes Idaho and at least one other adjoining state or Canadian province.

regularly occurring: Occurrence of the species is consistent in Idaho (e.g., it may migrate in and out of the state, but it returns on at least an annual basis), i.e., occurs regularly within Idaho at a manageable level.

relict: A persistent remnant of an otherwise extinct flora or fauna or kind of organism. A relict (or relic) is an organism that at an earlier time was abundant in a large area but now occurs at only one or a few small areas.

ruderal: Vegetation found on human-disturbed sites, with no apparent recent historical natural analogs, and whose current composition and structure is not a function of continuous cultivation by humans and includes a broadly distinctive characteristic species combination, whether tree, shrub, or herb dominated. The vegetation is often dominated by nonnative and/or generalist native species that have expanded in extent and abundance due to the human disturbances (Faber-Langendoen et al. 2014). Ruderal ecosystems are generally not priorities for conservation for their own sake, though they may support rare species or function as important landscape connectors or matrices in reserves. S4: Apparently Secure: At a fairly low risk of extirpation in the jurisdiction due to an extensive range and/or many populations or occurrences, but with possible cause for some concern as a result of local recent declines, threats, or other factors.

div.head: S1. Critically
div.p: S5: Secure: At very low or no risk of extirpation in the jurisdiction due to a very extensive range, abundant populations or occurrences, with little to no concern from declines or threats.
sclerophyllous: A type of vegetation that is adapted to long periods of dryness and heat.
setback: A restriction area or minimum distance used to limit the effects of stressors on environmentally sensitive areas or critical wildlife habitat areas.

SH. Possibly Extirpated: Known from only historical records but still some hope of rediscovery. There is evidence that the species or ecosystem may no longer be present in the jurisdiction, but not enough to state this with certainty. Examples of such evidence include (1) that a species has not been documented in approximately 20 to 40 years despite some searching and/or some evidence of significant habitat loss or degradation;
(2) that a species or ecosystem has been searched for unsuccessfully, but not thoroughly enough to presume that it is no longer present in the jurisdiction.

species: Includes taxonomic species as well as selected subspecies, populations, evolutionarily significant units (ESU), distinct population segments (DPS), or other entities below the species level (hereafter species); for some taxa, multiple species assemblages may be identified for consideration rather than individual species.

spillover event: Occurs when a reservoir population with a high pathogen prevalence comes into contact with a novel host population, the pathogen is transmitted from the reservoir population into the novel population.

stakeholders: Those individuals, groups, or institutions that have a vested interest in or can influence the natural resources of Idaho and/or that potentially will be affected by SWAP activities and have something to gain or lose if conditions change or stay the same. Stakeholders are all those who need to be considered in achieving SWAP revision goals and whose participation and support are crucial to its success.

stream order: Stream order in hydrography deals with the hierarchy of streams from the source (or headwaters) downstream. monogr.title: Understory vegetation reflects fire history, topography, and soils. Tall understory shrubs, such as Rocky Mountain Maple, Western Serviceberry, and Curl-leaf Mountain-mahogany, are patchy, while mid-height Big Sagebrush, Antelope-brush, Mallow Ninebark, Shiny-leaf Spirea, snowberries, or Snowbrush Ceanothus are more widespread. Low shrubs, such as Kinnikinnick, Creeping Oregon-grape, Mountain-box, and Common Juniper, also occur. Graminoids are often abundant in the understory, especially Bluebunch Wheatgrass, Idaho Fescue, Pinegrass, and Geyer's Sedge, but also Spike-fescue, needlegrasses, Wheeler's Bluegrass, and Cheatgrass. Forbs can be conspicuous, including Arrowleaf Balsamroot, eriogonums, Heart-leaf Arnica, Sweet-cicely, Thick-leaved Peavine, Spreading Dogbane
